# Professional formatting checklist (all templates)

The FULL formatting checklist for client-facing design workbooks. The six headline rules live in
SKILL.md; this file is the complete list - apply every rule every time, and run this checklist
before any version goes out. The bar: **a novice reader - not a seasoned developer - can follow
the document without resizing a single column, cell, or font.** Standing principle: leave every
document better-formatted than you found it.

- **Text in a cell gets borders around it.** Populated content regions read as bordered tables, not floating text. Never leave a filled-in table region with missing gridlines.
- **Tabular content lives in real tables** - header row, one column per attribute, borders on every cell. Never clump multi-line prose vertically down a single column when the content is actually a list or table (classic offenders: Object Model and Process Flow tabs).
- **Ran out of template rows? INSERT rows carrying the table's formatting - and shift everything below down cleanly.** Overwriting the content beneath a table, or appending unformatted rows, are both defects.
- **Never lose the template's formulas or formatting when filling it** (e.g., Unit Testing status-summary formulas, conditional formatting). Fill INTO the template's structure; if a fill method drops them (openpyxl can), switch to COM or restore them explicitly, and verify against the blank template afterward.
- **Text fits or wraps** - no clipped values. Wrap long text and set row height, or widen the column. If a reviewer can't see it, it isn't documented.
- **One blank, unformatted row (no fill, no borders) between the bottom of each section and the next section's header.** Sections that touch read as one run-on block.
- **Consistent fonts and sizes per role** (title / section band / instruction / table header / data) - never mix ad-hoc formatting into a template's established style roles. When adding to an existing doc, clone the styles of the neighboring cells (see the style-cloning method in the 16-tab spec - hand-guessing styles produced broken palettes).
- **Yellow cells always carry their question**: an incomplete cell gets the FFFF00 fill AND text stating what's needed and the follow-up action, so the reader knows the next step without asking.
- **No silently blank template tables.** Every template table either gets populated (derive from existing design content where possible - e.g., a pages table from the wireframe screen list, endpoint tables from the object model) or gets one yellow row: "TBD - none identified thus far (<date>); update as the design progresses." A blank table is ambiguous between "none exist" and "nobody looked" - that ambiguity is what this rule kills. Revisit every TBD-none row at each version.
- **Hide gridlines outside the content area.** Turn OFF sheet-level gridline display on every tab (content regions carry explicit borders, so nothing readable is lost) - default gridlines stretching into the unused area (columns/rows beyond the content) read as unfinished. Where used cells expect the READER to type (e.g., blank unit-test rows), border a sensible working range so the expectation is visible; leave the rest clean.
- Always use 8-hex ARGB fills (`FFFF0000`) in openpyxl - 6-hex renders transparent.
- Column A stays a narrow spacer where the template uses one; content starts in B.
- **Embedded diagrams get their own clear block - never overlapping cell content.** A process-flow or wireframe image floats above the grid, so wherever it lands it covers whatever text is under it. Reserve space: place the image below its caption/Figure line with one blank spacer row, then push the tab's table(s) DOWN so their first row starts at least one blank row below the image's bottom edge (compute the image's displayed height in rows; insert rows to move the table and everything below it - preserving borders/formulas). No cell with text may sit beneath any image. Size images to the content-column width (~9-10 in, keep aspect ratio, no distortion, no spill off-page) and consistent across tabs. Re-verify by exporting the tab to PNG - an image-over-text overlap is invisible in the cell grid but obvious in the render. (Learned 2026-08-03 on a delivered app, v1.2: the process-flow and wireframe images sat on top of their tables.)
- **Embed the CURRENT render, not a stale one.** When a diagram's source (.drawio/.bmpr) has been revised, re-render before embedding - a stale render can carry problems the source already fixed (a delivered app, v1.2, embedded a pre-cleanup process-flow PNG with garbled, overlapping arrow labels while the canonical .drawio rendered clean).
- **Border continuity is checked, not assumed**: right and bottom edges are the classic misses - sweep every populated rectangular region for all four edges plus interior gridlines. Merged cells don't AutoFit - compute their row heights from text length x column width. One blank unformatted row between the last table and any template canvas/color band at the bottom of a tab.
- **Border UNIFORMITY within each table**: every interior cell of one table gets the identical border treatment (headers may differ, but uniformly). Mixed weights/partial borders inside one table read as sloppiness. And **spacer columns (like the narrow column A) are never bordered** - they're empty space, not table.
- **Table grids are dark and consistent - no light-gray grids.** Use black/automatic thin lines for table grids, and the OUTSIDE border matches the interior line weight and tone (a light-gray perimeter around a dark grid, or vice versa, reads as unfinished - standing house preference, 2026-08-03).
- **Template tabs that look alien get harmonized**: when a template's own tabs (e.g., BoW Unit Testing / QA Review) don't match the document's header/table styling, restyle them to match - preserving their formulas, dropdowns, and structure. Consistency across the document outranks raw template fidelity ("leave it better").
- **Final pass before any version goes out**: open every tab and check it with fresh eyes at 100% zoom - clipped text, missing borders, clumped columns, orphaned formatting, and lost formulas are what clients notice first. A programmatic border/row-height checker beats eyeballing; run one when the doc was edited programmatically.
